Issued at 315 AM EDT Wed Aug 26 2026

Convective/severe weather potential today will continue to be the 
primary forecast concern for the short term period.

Clouds are expected to increase from west to east this morning as a 
zone of low level warm/moist advection across 
Wisconsin/northern Illinois builds eastward aligning with a 
zone of stronger 800 mb positive theta-e advection. Convection 
early this morning is limited to portions of southwest Wisconsin
in closer proximity to cold frontal boundary and where some 
DPVA is ongoing in advance of an upper level low centered across
the arrowhead of Minnesota. Through the morning, expecting some
increase in low level forcing with a pre-frontal trough type 
feature shifting across the western Great Lakes. Some isolated- 
scattered convection is possible later this morning/early 
afternoon along this pre-frontal feature, particularly across 
NW Indiana into southwest Lower Michigan. Instability through 
early afternoon should be quite limited and not expecting any 
threat of severe weather through early afternoon if convection 
does develop.

The primary mid/upper level trough and stronger mid/upper level 
forcing should be across central/northern Lower MI today, but 
southern Lower Michigan/northern Indiana will be located on southern 
extent of mid/upper level height falls accompanying this trough. 
Some increase in deep layer shear is expected this morning as modest 
increases in 500 mb flow to 30-40 knots is expected resulting in 
increasing deep layer shear to around 30 knots. Some moderate MLCAPE 
on the order of 2000-2500 J/kg is possible this afternoon, but 
likely oriented in narrow axis just ahead of the cold front as mid 
level lapse rates across the area remain on the marginal side. Some 
question persists regarding the extent of destabilization with 
a possibility that some pre-frontal cloudiness/convection could 
prevent instability magnitudes from reaching this potential. 
There is also some question as initiation time and coverage of 
convection as low level convergence fields may be a bit more 
limited across the local area as stronger mid/upper level 
forcing remains just north of the local area. Combination of 
moderate instability potential near frontal zone and sufficient 
deep layer shear could support isolated-scattered severe 
thunderstorm risk this afternoon into early evening. Damaging 
wind gusts to 60 mph appear to be the primary threat given steep
0-3km lapse rates, but some isolated large hail is possible 
especially closer to convective initiation time. However, 
limited mid level lapse rates may limit the hail potential. 
Given instability/shear combination some supercell 
structure/isolated tornado potential is possible, although 
guidance has trended to a bit more veered nature to near sfc 
flow over past several runs which could limit low level helicity
from earlier indications. The primary severe risk still looks 
to be largely in the 19Z-02Z timeframe, and particularly through
00Z. 

Loss of connection to stronger sfc based instability should diminish 
intensity of frontal convection after 00Z or 01Z this evening. Some 
patchy fog development is possible late tonight into early Thursday 
morning behind the sfc front with weak low level height gradient and 
residual near sfc moisture likely remaining in place. Another weak 
mid level trough will dive southeast in wake of today's upper trough 
for Thursday keeping the local area in broad cyclonic flow. Some 
surface based instability should be present in the afternoon and 
some possibility of isolated showers could materialize. Have 
maintained silent 10-14 PoPs this cycle given rather nebulous mid 
level forcing, but it is possible some low PoPs will be needed 
Thursday PM in later cycles. 

Friday should bring dry conditions as mid level ridging across 
central CONUS builds eastward. Positioning of this ridge upstream of 
the area should keep a modifying low level thermal trough in place 
with another day of seasonable temperatures on Friday. The weekend 
still looks to feature warmer conditions as favored storm track 
remains across northern tier of CONUS resulting in dampening of the 
upstream ridge and eventual return of low level warm air/moisture 
advection. This pattern evolution should support eventual 
advection of some warm mid level temperatures across the 
southern Great Lakes and Ohio Valley. This leads to low 
confidence in instability profiles for the weekend into early 
next week. Some potential will exist for sfc frontal boundary 
to approach the region in this pattern, but confidence in depth 
of frontal lift is in question given background synoptic 
pattern. Thus, low chance/slight chance PoPs will be maintained 
for much of the days 4-7 period along with transition to above 
normal temps.
